title: Milestone: How Hollywood Made Movies
objective: After this level you can connect the invention of film, the craft of shooting and cutting, and the studio system into one picture of how a classic Hollywood film was made.
summary: The studio era put every step of a film inside one company, from stars under contract and the Production Code to the studio's own theaters, until the 1948 Paramount ruling.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one classic Hollywood film to the screen.
cards.body: Fifty levels ago, a film was still frames flickering past a lamp. By the 1930s it was a product made on an assembly line, and one company could own every step. Here's the whole chain in one picture.

cards.headline: One film, one company, every step
cards.body: In the studio era, from about 1930 to 1945, a major studio carefully controlled every stage of a feature, from the first idea to the theater. Stars on seven-year contracts played the parts. The Production Code office had to approve the film. The studio's own distributors rented it out, often by the block, and its own first-run theaters showed it, at 24 frames a second, to paying crowds.

mascot.line: It connects: every level in this chapter is one link in that chain. Pull one link, and the rest move.

events.label: The Jazz Singer's success pushes Hollywood into sound
The Production Code Administration starts approving films
Citizen Kane's deep focus and flashbacks
The Paramount ruling; studios must sell their theaters

cards.headline: Milestone: the studio era, assembled
learned: Why a stack of still frames looks like motion, and how a projector shows them at a steady 24 a second.
How silent filmmakers built an industry in Hollywood and a film language of close-ups, crosscutting and montage.
How a scene is planned, framed, lit and cut so that space and time seem unbroken.
How a studio made, sold and showed a film by itself, and why the 1948 ruling broke that chain.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from the studio era in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: The Jazz Singer came in 1927, the Production Code Administration began in 1934, Citizen Kane in 1941, HUAC's hearings in 1947, the Paramount ruling in 1948 and CinemaScope with The Robe in 1953.

questions.prompt: Why does a strip of still frames look like smooth movement on screen?

options.label: Each image lingers on the retina and blends into the next
options.rationale: That's persistence of vision, the older, oversimplified story: blended images would pile up, not move.

options.label: Your brain reads small shifts between stills as motion
The projector slides the film smoothly past the lamp
options.rationale: A projector stops each frame to show it, then pulls the next one down.

options.label: Each frame is a blurred photograph of the movement
options.rationale: Each frame is a still; the motion isn't in any single one.

questions.explanation: Apparent motion, such as beta movement, makes a series of stills, each slightly shifted, look like one moving object. Persistence of vision is the older, oversimplified explanation.

questions.prompt: Why did independent filmmakers move from the East Coast to Hollywood in the 1910s?

options.label: The Trust had banned filming in New York
options.rationale: The Trust licensed patents and film stock; it couldn't ban a city.

options.label: Sound stages there were already built for talkies
options.rationale: Talkies arrived more than a decade later.

options.label: The studios owned every theater back East
options.rationale: Studio theater chains came in the 1920s, after the move.

options.label: Sun, cheap land and distance from the Trust

questions.explanation: Southern California offered year-round filming, varied scenery and cheap land and labor, and it is generally thought that its distance from the Trust's New York headquarters helped too.

questions.prompt: Some choices give a shot more depth of field. How did Gregg Toland get Citizen Kane's deep focus?

options.label: Telephoto lenses with wide-open apertures and soft light
options.rationale: Those choices give less depth of field, not more.

options.label: A rack focus pulled between near and far in each shot
options.rationale: Rack focus shifts sharpness from one plane to another; Toland kept both sharp at once.

options.label: Wide-angle lenses, small apertures and bright arc lamps
Shallow focus and dim, low-key lighting throughout
options.rationale: Shallow focus keeps only one plane sharp.

questions.explanation: Bright light, a narrow aperture and a wide-angle lens all give more depth of field. Toland used all three, with faster film, to keep near and far sharp.

questions.prompt: A scene cuts back and forth between two friends in a diner booth. What does the 180-degree rule ask of the camera?

options.label: Show both friends side by side in every shot of the scene
options.rationale: Close shots of one face are fine; what matters is which side the camera is on.

options.label: Stay on one side of the line running between them
Circle the table in a single unbroken take
options.rationale: The rule is about cutting between shots, not avoiding cuts.

options.label: Switch to the opposite side with every new cut
options.rationale: That's crossing the line, which flips the left-right geography.

questions.explanation: Keeping the camera on one side of the axis of action keeps each friend in the same area of the frame, so the room's left-right map never flips.

questions.prompt: Which link of the studios' make-ship-show chain did the 1948 Paramount decrees cut away?

options.label: Showing: the studios' theater chains
Making: the studios' sound stages
Starring: the seven-year contracts
options.rationale: Contracts were de Havilland's fight, not this case.

options.label: Approving: the Production Code office

questions.explanation: The decrees forced the majors to sell their theater chains, separating production from exhibition.

questions.prompt: A film is a series of still photographs. What did each frame of a three-strip Technicolor film start out as?

options.label: One photograph colored by hand after filming
options.rationale: The color came from dyes in printing, not paint.

options.label: A drawing traced from a filmed scene
A single full-color photograph on one strip of film
options.rationale: The camera held only black-and-white film.

options.label: Three black-and-white records of the same shot

questions.explanation: A beam-splitter sent the same image to three black-and-white strips, one each for red, green and blue.
